title: Garfield Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Garfield wells have a 124-foot median depth, 14 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $14,100-$24,400.
h1: Garfield, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
For rural property around Garfield in Chaffee County, the local well record is generally favorable, but the permit file is not a guarantee for a specific lot. Records within 5 miles show a median completed depth of 124 feet and a median reported yield of 14.0 gallons per minute. Most permitted wells serve domestic or household use, and most are identified with unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers.

The useful comparison is between the local statistics and the ground under the parcel. Garfield sits in mountain terrain where granite, gneiss, and fractured bedrock can change quickly across short distances. Check nearby wells, confirm the proposed well location, and have a driller price the actual access, casing, pump, trenching, and electrical work before you commit.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Garfield?
sections.html:
Garfield-area wells have a median reported depth of 124 feet. The middle half runs from 76 to 199 feet, so a driller bidding a typical residential well will usually be working in that range, while still allowing for a materially deeper hole. The 90th-percentile depth is 270 feet, and the deepest record reaches 500 feet.

Depth records are concentrated between 100 and 300 feet, which accounts for 64% of wells. Another 32% are under 100 feet, while 5% fall between 300 and 600 feet. Only 130 of the 178 permitted wells report a total depth, so these figures are a planning guide rather than a promise. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce water at different depths on neighboring lots.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Garfield well make?
sections.html:
Among the 73 Garfield-area wells reporting pump yield, the median is 14.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 34% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No recorded well in this set is listed below 1 gallon per minute.

That is a stronger local yield profile than many mountain areas, but it is still not a guarantee for an unbuilt well. A reported pumping yield is a test result for one well, not a permanent promise of household supply. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, and any production history. A domestic permit also has specific legal limits; an augmentation plan may be needed for uses beyond the permitted right.

sections.heading: What does the water table show near Garfield?
sections.html:
The median static water level is 34 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 22 to 50 feet. That gives a useful expectation for pump and casing planning, but the water level can vary with season, recharge, pumping, and the exact bedrock fracture reached by the well.

The decade comparison does not show a simple decline in these records. The median measured depth to water was 42 feet in the 2010s and 20 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later measurements were shallower on this dataset. Only 26 wells report a static water level, however, and the measured wells may not represent the same locations or conditions. Treat the series as local context, not proof of a rising regional water table.

sections.heading: Who has drilled wells near Garfield?
sections.html:
Permit records show activity across several decades, with 5 permits in the 1950s, 2 in the 1960s, 11 in the 1970s, 15 in the 1980s, 25 in the 1990s, 44 in the 2000s, 32 in the 2010s, and 21 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Most use is domestic or household use, accounting for 87% of permits.

American Drilling Service, listed with Dewberry, Bradford W., appears on 85 records. Bill Mccoy Enterprises, listed with Mccoy, William C., appears on 11, and High Peaks Well & Pump, listed with Jones, Allen, appears on 7. These are permit-record patterns, not endorsements. Confirm current licensing, availability, access requirements, and the scope of each written bid before hiring.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost in Garfield?
sections.html:
Local drilling conditions are fractured mountain bedrock, described as granite and gneiss. The drilling model uses a rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 124-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $8,100 to $12,400.

A finished well costs more than the hole. The local estimate for a completed system, including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is $14,100 to $24,400 at that median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, ledge, water storage, or long utility runs can move the bid higher. Have the contractor separate drilling, casing, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permits so competing estimates cover the same work.

sections.heading: What risks should a Garfield buyer check?
sections.html:
Water quantity is only one part of due diligence. Within about 10 miles are 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 628 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped locations do not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but they are a reason to review the well location, drainage, land-use history, and available water tests before closing.

Ask for testing appropriate to the property and its surroundings, including basic potability testing and any site-specific concerns identified by the records. Also check septic setbacks, replacement-area needs, driveway access, and the building site before drilling. A good yield does not remove the need for proper casing and grout, a compliant septic design, and enough space for construction and future maintenance.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Garfield
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit file for the parcel and nearby properties, not only a seller's verbal estimate. Compare wells in Garfield with records near Maysville, 4 miles away, and use the broader context around Poncha Springs, Pitkin, Smeltertown, Salida, and Nathrop when local records are thin. Neighboring wells can help reveal likely depth, yield, water level, and drilling conditions, but they do not replace a site-specific investigation.

Before buying, make the contract contingent on reviewing well construction, pump testing, water quality, and septic information. Before building, confirm the legal use of the permit, access for a rig, electrical routing, tank location, and the full site-development cost. In fractured bedrock, keep a realistic allowance for a deeper hole or an unsuccessful drilling result rather than treating the median as a guaranteed outcome.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Garfield, Colorado?
faq.a: Wells within 5 miles of Garfield have a median reported depth of 124 feet. The middle half is 76 to 199 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 270 feet. The deepest record is 500 feet. Since only 130 of 178 permits report total depth, use these figures for planning, not as a guarantee for a particular parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Garfield, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 124-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,100 to $12,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $14,100 to $24,400. Access, depth, casing, and utility distance can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a well produce in Garfield?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 14.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty percent of reporting wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 34% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These results come from 73 wells and do not guarantee a new well's production.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Garfield, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from yield or depth alone. Records show 3 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, along with 628 historic mine features. Those are screening flags, not proof of impact on a parcel. Test the specific well, review site history, and retest when local conditions warrant.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a property on a well near Garfield?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, construction report, pump test, static water level, and water-quality results. Garfield's median static water level is 34 feet below ground, and the middle half is 22 to 50 feet, but only 26 wells report that measurement. Also confirm septic setbacks, access for drilling equipment, legal well use, and room for future maintenance.
